title: CLO 2025 Academic Month  Group Collaboration to Inspire Digital Fashion Imagination
description: CLO 2025 Official Academic Monthly Course Review is now online! Lecturer Yu Si from China Academy of Art progressively analyzes the potential development of digitalization in the fashion field, as well as how 3D teaching and research combined with team projects stimulate students' potential.
transcript:
I am very happy to be able to share with you some of our discussions about the future development direction and possibilities in the digital fashion field, and I am also very grateful for the invitation from the organizer.

The topic I am going to share with you today is about the imagination of digital fashion, and since the moderator has just introduced it, I won’t go into too much detail.

Our course is actually a special design course for the third year at the China Academy of Fine Arts, and it is also the first time in recent years that the China Academy of Fine Arts has opened a fashion design school.

In this course, the students do not have any software-based skills. Previously, they did not take any courses related to software. This course lasts about seven weeks.

How to guide students in this limited time of seven weeks? It is a relatively big challenge for us to create a multidimensional project based on these students who have no software background.

Additionally, we are designing the initial curriculum for this course. The core issue of this first term course is the possibility of digitalization in the future of the fashion field.

We use a very mature and widely used app. We want to combine these digital, virtual, and different directions to explore whether there are more possibilities beyond virtual fashion, virtual showrooms, or commercial brands.

Moreover, we chose to use teamwork to teach the form and address the problems that appear throughout our entire workflow and work process.

First of all, we lead students to learn about the historical origins of digital fashion, cultural evolution, technical development, and the impact of artificial intelligence on future fashion trends, in order to open students’ imagination in the information age and foster a new understanding of fashion design.

This course aims to break down the concepts of digital media and the real physical world and to transform digital fashion design into an imaginative collection for students. It systematically establishes students’ creative thinking logic in personal digital fashion design and enables them to complete digital fashion series and display digital application scenarios through collaborative cooperation by learning from the aforementioned software.

Next, we can first introduce a relatively complete presentation of the final work from this group.

Hey, is there sound?  
A sound world.  
Are there any aspects one can analyze from this work?  
How can what one is seeing be related to what is happening in the present?

Buh-bye, Bowie. (repeated several times)

This approach will be more targeted to help students complete their projects.

In the process of learning software, we also integrate one-to-one counseling. Percy and I mainly focus on the students’ project development and the final form and content they produce.

At the final presentation in the seventh week, we held a small exhibition at the school. Some groups focused more on food interaction, while others concentrated on virtual interaction.

In the video we just saw, they focused more on virtual interaction and presented different forms of content produced for various projects.

These are some of our teachers. They are all artists and professional designers who have been growing in the fashion industry for many years.

Percy is a modern and advanced digital artist. He is mainly responsible for teaching AIGC and Nomad.

Yaya created a brand called Elter, which is a virtual fashion brand. At the time, he worked at VVS Westwood, the design headquarters in London, as a 3D fashion designer. He has also brought virtual fashion into the industry, whether through his own brand or current luxury brands, and he is a designer with real industry experience.

Mr. Qi Haoran is a teacher specializing in C4D scene modeling, and Mr. Maruyama is responsible for interaction design. Because in each project, there is actual interaction among participants.

This interaction between people, and between applications, has been part of Mr. Ma’s teaching experience for nearly ten years.

During our entire interaction teaching process, he mentioned that there were many problems he had not encountered in his years of teaching, because our students have no software foundation. They have no limits or expectations regarding what they can or cannot do.

So the whole process involves guiding their imagination towards a final output, and then the teachers provide software support based on the effect they want to achieve.

At the very beginning of the class, we held a large lecture during which each teacher shared insights from their field of deep learning, current developments, and future possibilities.

The mini-project in the first week involved projects produced after just one week of software learning.

Following that was the group project, which involved teamwork.

Why use group projects? Why teamwork?

First, due to the objective condition I mentioned earlier: students have no software foundation and lack the equipment to carry out certain tasks, especially rendering.

During production, some students had to go to a friend’s game company to borrow a high-spec computer for rendering. There were many interruptions due to such situations.

Second, teamwork serves as a preview of future social skills, such as dealing with interpersonal relationships in teamwork, how to maximize both personal value and team value.

Sometimes, individual ideas must serve the team, requiring compromise and balance.

Students learn how to find their own role in the team.

They may encounter team members lacking certain skills, like programming, which could necessitate adjustments to the final form of the project.

Others may not be good at digital design, but their team’s plan may involve producing interactive clothing or food items.

For example, interaction between food and people at the scene.

We also encountered a problem with the group project: since some industry mentors have their own companies, projects, or brands, they sometimes cannot teach on-site and must conduct online teaching.

At the beginning of the course, we arranged online resources and provided students with online course links so they could independently mobilize their motivation to learn software.

When the whole project is guided, a core point I discussed with Professor Percy is that this virtual digital world differs from the real world. It has no limitations, unlike the real world’s view and structure.

This allows for subversive design.

We hope students spread their own imagination and creativity to create a new worldview and structure.

At the beginning, we saw a video presentation of a team project about an upside-down world, a world opposite to the real world.

This was their prior research, explaining some of the meanings behind the upside-down concept.

This is a draft design of the entire computer-generated world at that time.

It resembles a multidimensional cube.

Since there are four students, they made four rooms, each with its own story.

These are the students’ designs of virtual clothing.

You can see that each student has a very strong personality.

This is the first student’s room. She is a sensitive and warm-hearted girl who focuses on themes related to her childhood and family.

In terms of clothing, she mainly applies Qo3D technology.

This is the second part of the clothing, the third student’s clothing, and the design of each room.

They have two different works for hand-studies.

The first is very unique.

This is the figure of the second student, and this is the figure of the third student.

The third student is very active.

This is the figure of the fourth student.

Then, this is some of their on-site food interaction.

We can see a spectator waving their hand in front.

When the hand waves, the patterns projected onto the clothing and scene change according to the movement.

On the right, they created a small interactive accessory and device.

The lighting flow rate and speed change according to the wearer’s heartbeat, sensed by touch.

I did not include the video for this.

This is another group’s student work.

Next is an overview of each project.

The first group combined traditional patterns with modern interactive forms.

We can see the poetry-inspired designs on the bottom left, which combine traditional and contemporary elements.

It is actually more of an application of AIGC, specifically Stable Diffusion software, for training and production.

Each student used their own drawings and designs to build a personal database.

Then Stable Diffusion generated more design possibilities in their style.

The middle project is an analysis of a case we began, focusing on purely virtual history and virtual interaction.

The two groups on the right: the upper group produced the heart rate interaction device we just shared.

The group below applied 3D projection and virtual generation interaction design.

Thank you!

chunks.content: # CLO 2025 Academic Month: Group Collaboration to Inspire Digital Fashion Imagination This document covers the development and teaching approach of a digital fashion design course at the China Academy of Fine Arts, focusing on digital fashion imagination, teamwork, software learning, and innovative project outcomes using advanced digital tools and concepts. --- ## Course Overview and Objectives This section introduces the digital fashion design course at the China Academy of Fine Arts, outlining its unique challenges, curriculum goals, and the integration of digital technologies in fashion education. The course is designed for third-year students at the newly established fashion design school within the China Academy of Fine Arts. It spans seven weeks and targets students without prior software skills. The core challenge is to guide these students—who lack any software background—through multidimensional digital fashion projects within a limited timeframe. The curriculum emphasizes exploring the future possibilities of digitalization in fashion beyond just virtual fashion, virtual showrooms, or commercial brands. It incorporates teamwork to address workflow challenges and enhance collaborative skills. Students begin by studying the historical origins of digital fashion, cultural evolution, technical developments, and the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on fashion trends. This foundation aims to broaden their imagination and foster a new understanding of fashion design in the digital age. The ultimate goal is to dismantle the boundaries between digital media and the physical world, enabling students to create imaginative digital fashion collections and demonstrate digital application scenarios through collaborative design work. --- ## Teaching Approach and Teamwork Structure This section details the pedagogical methods, software tools used, and the rationale behind using group projects to overcome technical limitations and enhance social skills. The course employs widely used, mature digital fashion software, integrating digital, virtual, and interactive elements. One-to-one counseling supports individual project development, focusing on both the conceptual and technical aspects. Teamwork is central to the course due to two main reasons: 1. **Technical Constraints:** Many students lack access to high-end equipment, such as computers capable of rendering complex digital designs. Some students had to borrow equipment from friends in gaming companies, causing workflow interruptions. 2. **Social and Professional Skill Development:** Team projects imitate future workplace scenarios, requiring students to negotiate roles, compromise on ideas, and maximize both personal and collective value. Teams often face skill imbalances, such as a lack of programming expertise, demanding adaptability in project scope and outcomes. The course also accommodates remote teaching when industry mentors cannot be on site. Online resources and course links are provided to ensure students can self-motivate and continue learning software independently. --- ## Faculty and Industry Expertise This section introduces the teaching staff and their roles, highlighting their industry experience and areas of specialization in digital fashion. - **Percy:** A modern digital artist responsible for teaching AI-generated content (AIGC) and the Nomad software. - **Yaya:** Founder of the virtual fashion brand *Elter* and former 3D fashion designer at VVS Westwood in London.

chunks.content: Online resources and course links are provided to ensure students can self-motivate and continue learning software independently. --- ## Faculty and Industry Expertise This section introduces the teaching staff and their roles, highlighting their industry experience and areas of specialization in digital fashion. - **Percy:** A modern digital artist responsible for teaching AI-generated content (AIGC) and the Nomad software. - **Yaya:** Founder of the virtual fashion brand *Elter* and former 3D fashion designer at VVS Westwood in London. Yaya brings real industry experience in virtual fashion design for both personal and luxury brand projects. - **Qi Haoran:** Specialist in Cinema 4D (C4D) scene modeling. - **Mr. Maruyama:** Expert in interaction design with nearly ten years of teaching experience focusing on user and application interaction in digital projects. The diverse expertise of the teaching team supports a comprehensive learning experience that spans artistic creativity, technical software skills, and interactive design. --- ## Curriculum Structure and Project Workflow This section outlines the weekly progression of the course and the types of projects students undertake, emphasizing early software learning and collaborative group work. The course begins with an introductory lecture where instructors share insights on deep learning, current digital fashion developments, and future possibilities. - **Week 1:** Mini-projects are created after only one week of software training, encouraging rapid skill acquisition. - **Weeks 2-7:** Students work in groups on multidimensional digital fashion projects that integrate virtual interaction, AI, and digital design. Group projects foster the development of social skills, role adaptation, and solving technical challenges collectively. The projects range from virtual clothing design and interactive food experiences to the creation of wearable devices that respond to biometric data. --- ## Digital Fashion Imagination: Multidimensional Virtual Worlds This section describes a representative group project that explores an "upside-down world," illustrating the students’ imaginative digital fashion design concepts and virtual environments. The project envisions a multidimensional cube representing a virtual world opposite to reality. Four students collaboratively designed four distinct rooms, each telling a unique story reflecting their personalities: - The first student, a sensitive and warm-hearted individual, focused on childhood and family themes, applying Qo3D (a 3D digital fashion technology) in her clothing designs. - Other students contributed diverse digital clothing and virtual environments, showcasing strong personal style. Interactive elements include: - **Food Interaction:** On-site installations where spectators’ hand movements trigger changes in projected patterns on clothing and surroundings. - **Wearable Devices:** Accessories that sense the wearer’s heartbeat via touch, dynamically adjusting lighting flow and speed in real time. These immersive interactions illustrate the fusion of physical and digital elements in digital fashion design. --- ## Project Examples and Technical Applications This section summarizes various student projects demonstrating the use of AI-generated content and interactive digital technologies. - One group combined traditional cultural patterns with modern interactive forms, producing poetry-inspired designs. - Students utilized AI-generated content (AIGC) tools like *Stable Diffusion* to expand their personal design databases, generating new fashion possibilities aligned with their unique styles.

These projects showcase the practical application of AI, 3D modeling, and interaction design in creating innovative digital fashion experiences. --- # Summary This course at the China Academy of Fine Arts offers a pioneering approach to digital fashion education by integrating cultural, technical, and interactive elements within a collaborative framework. It equips students without prior software experience to create imaginative digital fashion projects that blend AI, 3D design, and user interaction, preparing them for the evolving digital fashion industry.
